briefing.text: Whether a pathway is 'significantly mutated' is a statistical question. The percent of samples with any pathway mutation does not answer it, because large gene sets made of long genes get hit by chance. Count the samples with at least one nonsilent mutation in the pathway genes and compare that count with a null model that accounts for each sample's mutation count and each gene's coding length (for example, permute each sample's mutations across genes weighted by CDS length, or run per-sample binomial tests and combine them PathScan-style). Make the call from the null-model p-value. A high raw frequency with p>0.05 does not contradict 'not significantly mutated'.
briefing.reason: This sets the evidence standard for the label. Without it, a team could read a high raw mutation frequency as significance.

briefing.text: The result depends heavily on which genes define ERBB-PI3K. Write the gene list out. Use a narrow curated set as the primary test: EGFR, ERBB2, ERBB3, ERBB4, PIK3CA, PIK3CB, PIK3R1, PIK3R2, PTEN, AKT1, AKT2, AKT3, MTOR, TSC1, TSC2, RICTOR, RPTOR, STK11, INPP4B and PPP2R1A, which is the TCGA 2018 PI3K set plus the ERBB receptors. Then rerun with a broader KEGG ErbB set as a sensitivity check. If the two disagree, report the curated result as primary and note the difference.
briefing.reason: How the gene set is defined can flip the conclusion, so it needs to be fixed in advance and checked for sensitivity.

briefing.text: Count only nonsilent coding variants as pathway hits: Missense, Nonsense, Frame_Shift, In_Frame, Splice_Site, Translation_Start_Site and Nonstop (check the Variant_Classification column in data_mutations.txt). Leave out silent, intronic, UTR, flank and other non-coding variants. Silent variants can be used to estimate the background rate.
briefing.reason: Including non-coding or silent variants inflates the number of pathway hits.

briefing.text: data_mutations.txt has a FILTER column (with values such as 'common_variant') and population-frequency columns (ExAC_AF, GMAF). Leftover germline polymorphisms, which are common in Asian-ancestry cohorts that reference panels cover poorly, can look like recurrent pathway mutations. Exclude calls flagged common_variant and calls with population AF above 1% (including ExAC_AF_EAS). Be wary of variants that recur at the same position in many samples but are not known hotspots. Rerun the test after filtering.
briefing.reason: Germline artefacts can make the pathway look falsely significant.

briefing.text: Sample IDs do not match between tables: the clinical table uses IDs like 'NPC15F' while Tumor_Sample_Barcode in the MAF uses IDs like 'NPC015D'. Compare the two ID sets and normalise the formats. Use all sequenced samples in data_clinical_sample.txt as the denominator, including any with zero mutations, not only the samples that appear in the MAF.
briefing.reason: A naive join drops samples and changes the denominator for frequency and significance.

briefing.text: Check whether any patient has more than one sample (compare unique PATIENT_ID with SAMPLE_ID, and look for suffixes that mark repeat samples). If so, keep one sample per patient before testing the pathway.
briefing.reason: Counting repeat samples from the same patient inflates recurrence.

briefing.text: One or a few hypermutated tumours can carry most of the pathway mutations. Look at mutations per sample (and TMB if it is available) and at what share of pathway hits comes from the top 1-3 samples. Count samples mutated rather than total mutations, use a per-sample null, or report the result with hypermutators excluded.
briefing.reason: Hypermutators can drive a false significant result.

briefing.text: The only molecular data here are point mutations and indels; there is no copy-number file. Published ERBB-PI3K alteration rates often include amplifications, which these data cannot show. Frame the test as mutation-level significance. Mutation data are enough to test 'significantly mutated', so a missing CNA file is not by itself grounds for 'Not verifiable'.
briefing.reason: This prevents a wrong 'Not verifiable' call and stops teams comparing these data with published rates that include copy-number alterations.

briefing.text: Record how many pathway or gene-set tests you run. If you test several, apply Benjamini-Hochberg and treat ERBB-PI3K as significant only if q<0.05. If it is the single pre-specified test, use p<0.05. Fisher-combined p-values are anti-conservative when their inputs are correlated.

Check how the coding lengths of your pathway genes compare with those of your random sets. Does a length- and burden-aware null change your method or label?

Which test is your single pre-specified primary test, how robust is it to plausible alternative backgrounds (e.g. gene-specific rates or a different universe), and does that change your label or your confidence?

referee.difference: Same data and filters; both find 5/56 samples hit in the strict ERBB+PI3K/AKT/mTOR set (borderline, p~0.09-0.12). X reads 'significantly mutated' as a pure length-weighted recurrence test on the strict set (or the broad ~80-gene KEGG set, p=0.25) and discounts hotspots -> True. Y includes RAS (KEGG ErbB core) giving 7/56 hit, and counts the recurrent canonical activating hotspots -> False.
referee.test: referee_test.py: (1) per-sample burden- and protein-length-aware null (11.5M aa proteome) for strict set and strict+KRAS/NRAS/HRAS; (2) hotspot-codon enrichment: number of nonsilent missense calls landing on 22 canonical activating codons in pathway genes (KRAS/NRAS/HRAS 12/13/61, PIK3CA 542/545/1047, ERBB2, EGFR, AKT1 E17, ERBB3 V104) vs Poisson expectation, with 1x/10x/100x mutability inflation.
referee.expected_if_x: If X is right (pathway mutations are passenger-level noise), hits at canonical activating codons should be at chance level (~0-1, p not small even with modest mutability inflation) and the RAS-including recurrence test should be non-significant.
referee.expected_if_y: If Y is right, pathway hits should be concentrated on canonical activating hotspots far beyond chance, and the RAS-including core set should be significantly recurrent.
referee.outcome: Strict set: 5/56 vs 2.49 expected, p=0.089. Strict+RAS: 7/56 vs 2.55 expected, p=0.011. Hotspot test: 3 observed (PIK3CA E545K, KRAS G12V, NRAS Q61R) vs 0.0026 expected, p=2.9e-9; p=2.4e-3 even at 100x mutability. Only 2 codons in the whole MAF are hit in two samples, so canonical-hotspot hits are not a generic artefact.
referee.reason: Pathway mutations are far from passenger noise: canonical activating hotspots are enriched by orders of magnitude, and the core ERBB-RAS-PI3K set is significantly recurrent under a burden-aware null. Only X's strict no-RAS, hotspot-blind definition gives a non-significant result, and even that is borderline (p~0.09). The evidence contradicts 'not significantly mutated', so the label is False.

findings.question: How do standard pathway-level mutation significance methods (e.g. PathScan, MutSig-style gene-set tests, Hotnet-type approaches) define the background model, and specifically how do they account for gene coding length and per-sample mutation burden?
findings.answer: They use a background-mutation-rate (BMR) null that accounts for gene length and usually for each sample's mutation burden. PathScan tests each sample separately: it computes the probability of the observed number of mutated pathway genes under random mutation at background rate rho, with each gene's hit probability set by its length. It then combines the per-sample p-values by Fisher-Lancaster. MutSig/MutSigCV scores mutations against a patient-specific background rate over each gene's covered bases, with gene-specific covariates (expression, replication time). Weighted-resampling pathway methods (Jia & Zhao 2012) weight each gene by the individual's BMR times gene length. Naive hypergeometric tests that treat all genes equally are described as biased toward pathways of long genes. So the standard is a null that accounts for both length and burden. I did not read a HotNet source, so this answer does not cover HotNet-type methods.

findings.question: In gene-set permutation tests on somatic mutation data, what gene universe is conventionally used (all genes in the exome, genes on the sequencing target, or only genes observed mutated), and how does the choice bias the result?
findings.answer: The convention is the sequenced territory: all genes in the exome or on the capture target, weighted by their covered coding length. MutSig tabulates covered bases per gene and patient, and PathScan uses gene lengths under an exome-wide BMR. None of the sources I read use a universe of only the genes observed mutated. My reasoning, not stated by any source: restricting to mutated genes conditions on the outcome and discards the length and burden information the null needs, so results from it are not comparable to standard tests. A whole-exome or target universe with length weighting is the defensible version. The pages I read do not settle exactly how large or in which direction the bias is.

findings.question: In commonly used cancer pathway definitions (e.g. TCGA pan-cancer oncogenic signaling pathways, KEGG ErbB), are RAS genes such as KRAS and NRAS counted as part of an 'ERBB-PI3K' pathway or as a separate RTK-RAS pathway?
findings.answer: It depends on the definition. KEGG ErbB signaling (MSigDB KEGG_ERBB_SIGNALING_PATHWAY, 87 genes) includes KRAS, NRAS and HRAS, along with EGFR, ERBB2-4, the PIK3 subunits, AKT1-3 and MTOR. TCGA pan-cancer (Sanchez-Vega et al., Cell 2018) puts KRAS, NRAS and HRAS in the RTK-RAS pathway together with the ERBB receptors, and treats PI3K/Akt as a separate pathway. It has no combined 'ERBB-PI3K' pathway. An ERBB-PI3K set based on KEGG ErbB would therefore include RAS genes, and a TCGA-style set would not.
